line: Sat sri akal. Harjit Singh. Thirty-one years I drove a truck, coast to coast. Now I drive to the gurdwara, the park, and here. Very short routes.
Everywhere. Interstate 80, mostly. Best pie in Nebraska, worst coffee in Wyoming. I still know the mile markers. My wife says I recite them in my sleep.
Some days. Now on Sundays I cook in the langar at the gurdwara. Three hundred people, anybody can eat. Last month two firefighters came in. They came back with their wives.
Anybody. Cover your head, take off your shoes, sit on the floor. That's all. Come one Sunday. I'll put you on rotis. Everybody's first rotis are ugly.
My grandson Jaspreet plays baseball. Catcher. I go to every game. I still don't understand why the man who catches is the most tired.
Harjit has his phone propped on a water bottle. "Cricket. Melbourne, three in the morning there. My grandson says watch baseball. Baseball has too many pauses."
You listen to old men. That's rare. Twenty years on the road, I was the only turban at most truck stops. Most people were fine. Some days, not fine.
choice1: What did you do on those days?

line: My nephew drives a truck now. At a weigh station last week they checked his papers twice, then asked about his turban. He's from Fresno. Born there.
The president said something kind about Sikhs on TV. My wife made me watch it twice. Then she said, 'Now he has to do something.'
Every time I come for chai, you're here. Good. Mr. Deshpande likes you. He doesn't say so. He moves his chair to make room. That's how he says so.
Jaspreet says he saw you at the ball field with the other parents. Good. You can explain to me what is a 'balk.'
choice1: Nobody knows what a balk is.

line: Harjit nods and goes back to his phone.
Last over. If I look away now, they lose. It's my fault every time.
